We compare Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM, Kong, TrueFoundry, Cloudflare, Vercel, OpenRouter and Orq.ai on latency, pricing, licensing, governance and deployment. The post 9 Best AI Gateways in 2026: Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM, Kong and 5 More Ranked appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> An AI gateway is a control layer between your application and model providers. It gives every service one API for many models. It also centralizes routing, retries, failover, caching, budgets and logs. This guide presents the best AI gateways for production teams in 2026. The market moved fast this year. Palo Alto Networks closed its acquisition of Portkey on May 29. Mintlify acquired Helicone , which now runs in maintenance mode. LiteLLM survived a PyPI supply chain compromise in March. Your gateway choice now carries vendor and security risk, not just feature risk. TL;DR Best overall for self-hosted performance: Bifrost. Go binary, Apache 2.0, 11 µs published overhead at 5,000 RPS. Best open-source gateway with guardrails: Portkey. MIT license, 1,600+ models, now backed by Palo Alto Networks. Widest adoption: LiteLLM. 53.8K GitHub stars, 100+ providers, Python-first. Best for API platform teams: Kong AI Gateway. LLM, MCP and A2A traffic in one stack. Best managed options: Cloudflare (edge, free core), Vercel (zero markup), OpenRouter (model access). How We Ranked These AI Gateways We weighted 6 criteria for production use: Performance evidence: published overhead, and how it was measured. Coverage: providers and models behind one OpenAI-compatible API. Governance: virtual keys, budgets, RBAC, audit logs, guardrails. Deployment: self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped, or managed only. Cost model: markup, platform fees, free tier limits. Vendor and supply chain risk: license, ownership changes, security history. The post Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. How does OmniParseBench scoring work? The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: present: a text, number or equation appears (text) order: text A comes before text B (text) repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text) table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables) layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout) Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. What are the OmniParseBench launch results? Parser Headline Text Tables Layout Gemini 3.8 Flash* 92.9 91.3 95.2 92.2 Datalab accurate 92.7 90.8 91.8 95.6 Datalab balanced 91.6 90.0 89.2 95.5 Reducto 90.8 85.4 91.2 95.8 LlamaParse 90.4 88.2 92.6 90.4 Mistral OCR 89.5 82.8 91.9 93.8 Claude Sonnet 5.5* 88.7 93.1 95.4 77.5 GPT-5.6 Sol 87.8 85.4 91.6 86.5 Extend 83.3 64.1 92.5 93.4 Azure 83.0 74.6 81.7 92.8 Tesseract none 17.6 0.0 unsupported *Used in creating and verifying at least some tests, per Datalab . Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time. Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It flags the two models that helped build tests, and it tells readers to weigh the fact that it sells a parser. It commits to reporting OmniParseBench scores for future releases. Its advice: the best benchmark is your own documents. How do you run OmniParseBench? Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser uv pip install omni-parse-bench # score(): no network, no API keys uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[harness]' # + vendor adapters, to predict uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[benchmark]' # + dataset access, to run the benchmark opb benchmark --out runs/ --limit 5 --providers datalab openai/gpt-5.6-sol Vendors need keys such as DATALAB_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The CLI shows its plan and asks before calling any vendor. Runs are resumable. The query guide shows how to compare runs by tag, suite or test type. The post Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. How does OmniParseBench scoring work? The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: present: a text, number or equation appears (text) order: text A comes before text B (text) repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text) table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables) layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout) Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. What are the OmniParseBench launch results? Parser Headline Text Tables Layout Gemini 3.8 Flash* 92.9 91.3 95.2 92.2 Datalab accurate 92.7 90.8 91.8 95.6 Datalab balanced 91.6 90.0 89.2 95.5 Reducto 90.8 85.4 91.2 95.8 LlamaParse 90.4 88.2 92.6 90.4 Mistral OCR 89.5 82.8 91.9 93.8 Claude Sonnet 5.5* 88.7 93.1 95.4 77.5 GPT-5.6 Sol 87.8 85.4 91.6 86.5 Extend 83.3 64.1 92.5 93.4 Azure 83.0 74.6 81.7 92.8 Tesseract none 17.6 0.0 unsupported *Used in creating and verifying at least some tests, per Datalab . Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time. Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It flags the two models that helped build tests, and it tells readers to weigh the fact that it sells a parser. It commits to reporting OmniParseBench scores for future releases. Its advice: the best benchmark is your own documents. How do you run OmniParseBench? Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser uv pip install omni-parse-bench # score(): no network, no API keys uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[harness]' # + vendor adapters, to predict uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[benchmark]' # + dataset access, to run the benchmark opb benchmark --out runs/ --limit 5 --providers datalab openai/gpt-5.6-sol Vendors need keys such as DATALAB_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The CLI shows its plan and asks before calling any vendor. Runs are resumable. The query guide shows how to compare runs by tag, suite or test type. TL;DR What is […] The post Meet Grok Voice 3.0: SpaceXAI Voice Agent Model Ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0 . Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0. TL;DR Runs on: SpaceXAI’s hosted Voice Agent API only. No open weights, no local or quantized variants. Performance: Highest Index score of any model Artificial Analysis currently ranks. Best: 86.9 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index, ranked #1. Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. Bottom line: Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio. Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning. What is Grok Voice 3.0? Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks? The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%. Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%. Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0. Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here. τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap? Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable. TL;DR What is […] The post Meet Grok Voice 3.0: SpaceXAI Voice Agent Model Ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0 . Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0. TL;DR Runs on: SpaceXAI’s hosted Voice Agent API only. No open weights, no local or quantized variants. Performance: Highest Index score of any model Artificial Analysis currently ranks. Best: 86.9 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index, ranked #1. Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. Bottom line: Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio. Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning. What is Grok Voice 3.0? Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks? The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%. Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%. Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0. Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here. τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap? Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable. GPT-Live-1 costs $0.05 per minute, but backend model and tool usage is billed separately. Gemini 3.8 Live bills audio per minute plus text tokens. The System One model adds experimental image input, a Box bounding-box type and an opt-in 262k-token context, at $0.042 per million input tokens. The post TypeSafe AI Releases Jev 1.14 With Images, Box Type and 262k Context appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> TypeSafe AI has released Jev 1.14 , a new version of its System One decision model. It is live now under the jev-preview alias. It adds 3 experimental ‘danger zone’ features: images, a box type and longer context. For developers, Jev 1.14 pushes a typed decision model toward vision tasks like inspection and localization. TypeSafe shares a note that none of the 3 features are ready for production yet. TL;DR: Jev 1.14 Size: Parameters not disclosed. Context is 64k tokens per request and 32k per question by default, or 262k with an opt-in header. Runs on: TypeSafe’s hosted API only ( POST /v1/systemone ). No open weights. Hardware and quantized variants not disclosed. Performance: Small gains everywhere, largest in multilingual support (TypeSafe’s claim, no public scores). Best: In TypeSafe’s Box test, 4 edge-check questions caught 30 of 36 cut-off crops. Worst: Images and Box are not production-ready, and Box has no “not found” answer. What is Jev 1.14? Jev is a System One model from TypeSafe AI that returns typed decisions instead of generated text. You send a state along with typed questions : Choice, Score or Noul. Jev answers each with a typed value, probabilities and a confidence score. TypeSafe trains it with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) . The new version, jev-1.14.0 , brings small, subtle improvements to almost everything, according to the release post . TypeSafe expects the largest gain in multilingual support. How does image input work in Jev? Images are composable. Each image is listed once in a top-level assets map under a reference string. You then place that reference anywhere in state , instructions or criteria . The API swaps each reference for the image before the model reads it. TypeSafe says jev-1.13.0 was multimodal all along. Per the Images docs , both Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 now accept images. Each request needs the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true . Key image limits : PNG or JPEG still images only, up to 16 MiB per file 256 to 1568 pixels per side 32 MiB per request body Images bill as input tokens at the normal price, with no separate charge TypeSafe warns that all models, Jev included, perform worse on images than on pure text. It recommends the simplest possible questions. What is the new Box type? Box is a new question type that returns 1 bounding box per question. The answer gives top , bottom , left and right edges as fractions from 0 to 1. It also returns a confidence score. Box needs jev-1.14.0 or jev-preview , plus the images header. Box always returns a box. A question about an absent object still returns 4 edges. TypeSafe suggests pairing it with a Noul question that checks whether the target exists. TypeSafe also shared a small test on 36 painting crops, each cutting off part of the target. 4 per-edge Noul questions caught 30 cuts. A single “is all of it inside” question caught 26. Drawing the box as an outline and asking about it caught 20. How long is Jev’s context window now? By default, both models keep 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. Sending TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true raises both limits to 262k tokens, per the Models docs . TypeSafe states that Jev always supported longer context internally. It capped context on purpose because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on long inputs. The dev team still recommends short contexts. What do the benchmarks show? TypeSafe published internal intelligence charts in the release post . They compare Jev only against open-weight models. The post does not include a numeric score table. TypeSafe says the measurement is likely biased toward its own models. It tells developers to favor their own evals. Pricing, availability and migration Pricing is unchanged at $42 per billion input tokens, or $0.042 per million. Output tokens are free, per the Models docs . The rollout plan from the release post : jev-preview points to jev-1.14.0 now. jev-latest moves to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 stays available, with 60 days notice before deprecation. jev-1.14.0 will get 30 days notice before its own deprecation. How does Jev 1.14 compare? Feature Jev 1.14 Jev 1.13 Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite Model ID jev-1.14.0 jev-1.13.0 gemini-3.5-flash-lite Model type Typed decision model Typed decision model General LLM Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Default context 64k per request / 32k per question 64k per request / 32k per question 1,048,576 input tokens Long context 262k (opt-in header) 262k (opt-in header) Not applicable Image input Yes, experimental header Yes, experimental header Yes (text, images, video, audio, PDF) Bounding boxes Native box type, edges 0 to 1 No Prompted JSON box_2d , scaled 0 to 1000 ( docs ) Output Typed answers with confidence Typed answers with confidence Text, up to 65,536 tokens Input price (per 1M tokens) $0.042 $0.042 $0.30 Output price (per 1M tokens) Free Free $2.50 Status Preview ( jev-preview ) Stable ( jev-latest ) Stable Key Takeaways Jev 1.14 is live as jev-preview . jev-latest switches in a week. Images work on Jev 1.13 and 1.14 behind a danger-zone header. The new Box type returns 1 normalized bounding box per question. Long-context mode lifts limits to 262k tokens, at a reliability cost. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 14 Oct 2026 13:48:15 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Stella & Dot Founder Raises $5M For Her Next Act, AI Marketing Startup Marklo https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/founder-raises-5m-next-act-ai-marketing-startup-marklo-herrin/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 12:00:38 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94222 Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot , a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com , but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green , founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 14 Oct 2026 23:13:10 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 How To Build Your Team With Autonomous Humans, Not Just Autonomous Systems https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/building-autonomous-human-team-success-francia-uniplay/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 11:00:54 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94227 By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. That’s up about 50% from the prior quarter and tied for the highest quarterly tally in years, as charted below. The funding bump was due to larger rounds, not more of them. Round counts actually declined sequentially across all stages last quarter, Crunchbase data shows. Biggest cybersecurity fundraisers AI startups accounted for the overwhelming majority of cybersecurity funding, with a particular focus on identity security. Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter. Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider Keyfactor , which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners . Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage. Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners . The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion. Cyera , operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity -led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup. For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients. Exits, too We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish. Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age. It acquired Oasis Security , an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion. As for public offerings, Aura , which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut.
